claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has an intrinsic hierarchical heterostructure containing ordered and disordered phases, nanoprecipitates, and phase boundaries.
A machine-learning surrogate incorporating hierarchical heterostructure descriptors will accurately predict Young's modulus.
A machine-learning surrogate can predict yield strength from alloy-related inputs.
A machine-learning surrogate incorporating hierarchical heterostructure descriptors will accurately predict fracture behavior.
The proposed model will outperform established finite-element and CALPHAD-based simulations.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs load transfer in HfNbTiVAl10.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs plastic-deformation mechanisms in HfNbTiVAl10.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs crack-propagation paths in HfNbTiVAl10.
Quantified microstructural features correlate with the mechanical performance of HfNbTiVAl10.
By learning microstructure–property correlations, the surrogate can bypass computationally expensive iterative simulations.
The proposed model will attain an average prediction error below 10% for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior.
The proposed model will achieve at least a fivefold computational speedup relative to traditional simulations.
Standard finite-element and CALPHAD approaches typically have prediction errors above 15%.
Standard finite-element and CALPHAD approaches require longer computation times than the proposed surrogate.
Unexpected heterostructure evolution at extreme strain rates or temperatures may cause the model to fail.
Characterization noise or resolution limits may prevent reliable capture of key descriptors and cause prediction failure.
The chosen descriptors may not adequately capture sub-micron crack-propagation mechanisms.
The chosen descriptors may not adequately capture dynamic phase transformations.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome requires average error below 10%, but the error-based falsification rule triggers only above 15%. Thus an independently measured error from 10% through 15% would violate the quantitative prediction without meeting the declared falsification rule.
